Virovitica Old Jewish Cemetery

Jewish Cemetery · Virovitica, Croatia

Demolished. Virovitica, first recorded in 1234 and later under 120 years of Ottoman rule until 1684, grew into a multicultural trading hub of Croats, Germans, Hungarians, and Serbs. Jews arrived from Hungary in the 18th century, though a formal community only organized in the mid-19th century; an 1863 synagogue was among the first in Slavonia, funded partly by wealthy members who paid 300 forints for reserved seats. A Jewish school opened in 1875, teaching in both German and Hebrew. Population peaked around 2,854 regionally by the late 19th century but had fallen to 350 by 1940. During the Holocaust, over 160 local Jews were killed; Croatian nationalists destroyed the synagogue in 1942. Only 21 Jews remained after the war, never rebuilding the community; by 1996, just 16 Jews lived in Virovitica. Notable native son Miroslav Feldman (1899-1976) became a celebrated Croatian-Jewish writer known for socially critical, satirical works. This original cemetery, built in 1830 in nearby Antunovac, operated until 1870, when a new Virovitica cemetery replaced it (some graves were relocated); this older site was later completely abandoned and demolished.
